speechtext:
The Canadian beekeepers, as I indicated recently to the house, interviewed me about a week or ten days ago and stated the facts with regard to their industry. I made representations to the government, based upon the facts as the beekeepers presented them to me. They stated that they had a carryover of four million pounds of honey from the year 1947 into the year 1948, and that they had somewhere between 40 million and 45 million pounds of honey in the year 1948, with the result that there is a considerable carryover this year. speechtext:
May
I direct a question to the Minister of Transport? Can he inform the house of the circumstances surrounding a reported riot in Halifax this morning involving Canadian National Steamships? Were any persons injured? If so, how many, and in what manner were they injured?

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL STEAMSHIPS-SEAMEN'S UNION  INCIDENT AT HALIFAX
speechtext:
I am informed that about three a.m. today, 176 men boarded the steamships Challenger, Connector, and Lady Rodney, vessels of the Canadian National Steamships. On arrival these men were met by very few pickets, who dispersed immediately and allowed the newcomers to board three vessels of the Canadian National Steamships. The ships, being fully manned, began to move into the stream. By that time several hundred members of the Canadian seamen's union arrived on the docks and immediately grabbed the hoses in the sheds and played the streams on the men aboard the ships. However they were stopped by local harbour police from continuing this. Retaliation was made by the crews on the ships, who sprayed water on the men on the docks. Missiles were exchanged between the docks and the ships, such as stones, bottles and the like. It is also reported that several shots were fired; and I am advised that after investigation it appears that these shots were fired, first from the vessel and later from the shore. They were small pellets fired from guns, and some injuries are reported. I am informed, however, that no one was seriously hurt.
The situation at the present time is quiet on the harbour front in Halifax, and the vessels are at anchor in the harbour.

speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Agriculture, a copy of which I have sent to him. In view of current reports that grasshoppers are already hatching in Saskatchewan, and that federal government assistance to combat this menace is inadequate, will the federal government take immediate steps to increase financial and other aid to Saskatchewan in order to save this year's crops?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Gardiner (Minister of Agriculture):
subtopic: SASKATCHEWAN-INQUIRY AS TO FEDERAL ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
As I said a few days ago, the practice has been for provincial governments

to take care of the campaigns against grasshoppers. I have made inquiries since, and I find that in one year in the history of the battle against grasshoppers-and that was in the thirties, when western farmers were suffering from drought and depression generally-the federal government did give assistance in fighting grasshoppers. While I have not very many good things to say for the socialist government of Saskatchewan, I must say that up to date they have been fighting grasshoppers without asking for assistance from the federal government. This being so, I do not think there is any great necessity for our doing anything about it at the present time.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR MARKETING IN INTERPROVINCIAL AND EXPORT TRADE

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Gardiner (Minister of Agriculture) moved
subtopic: PROVISION FOR MARKETING IN INTERPROVINCIAL AND EXPORT TRADE
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 82, to provide for the marketing of agricultural products in interprovincial and export trade.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in moving the second reading of this bill I hope to confine myself to an historical review of what has led up to the bringing of it into the house.


I understand from the discussions which have taken place, not only during this session but during the last five or six sessions, that all groups in the house are in favour of legislation of this kind. Therefore I do not expect that there will be any great opposition to the bill. When we get into the committee stage some hon. members may wish to ask questions with respect to aspects of the measure which will not be sufficiently explained by what I have to say on the second reading.
I should like to take hon. members back to March 23, 1938. I have in my hand the submission which was made by what was then called the chamber of agriculture, which has since become the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, to the commission which was then examining into dominion-provincial relations. I refer to this in order to give a history of the development of the issue in the province in which the question has been dealt with to a greater extent than elsewhere; I refer to British Columbia. There are only three paragraphs in this document that I wish to read, but they will take us to the beginning of the historical review of the position. I quote:
A provincial act known as the Produce Marketing Act was passed by the province of British Columbia in 1927. This act was designed to control and regulate the marketing of certain agricultural products produced within a given area within the province, and it is apparent that the framers of that act relied upon the provisions of subsection 13 or subsection 16 or both, of section 92.
That was the British North America Act.
The act was, however, in 1930, declared to be ultra vires of the provincial legislature.
That was their first effort at passing legislation to control marketing within the province. The submission continues:
In 1934 the dominion parliament passed an act entitled the Natural Products Marketing Act, and it is apparent that the framers of that act relied upon the provisions of subsection 2 of section 91, "the regulation of trade and commerce." That act was in 1936 declared to be ultra vires of the dominion parliament.
In 1934 the province of British Columbia passed an act known as the Natural Products Marketing (B.C.) Act, and that act, after the dominion Natural Products Marketing Act had been declared to be ultra vires, was amended.
They amended their legislation in a manner which they thought would bring it within the powers of the legislature of the province, basing their amendments on the decision which had been given against the federal legislation. The submission continues:
The act as amended is now before the courts, and is to be carried to the privy council with a view to determining the authority of the province to pass the act.
That is the record in so far as it is shown in this document, and I think it is a complete

record of what had happened up to that moment.
All I wish to say in addition is that the British Columbia legislation was declared to be intra vires by the courts, right through to the privy council. After it had been declared to be intra vires, the British Columbia chamber of agriculture made an appeal to all the provinces in Canada to pass similar legislation, and they also made an appeal to the dominion government to pass enabling or complementary legislation. When representations were first made to this government we suggested that probably we would be well advised to await the actions of the provinces and to consider what should be done after we had had some experience with those acts.
The next representation which we had, following the proposal I have just referred to on the part of the province, came to us from the Canadian chamber of agriculture as a result of a meeting held in Winnipeg. I think I should place on the record the letter which was written to me on that occasion by the then secretary, Mr. George Coote, of the province of Alberta. He wrote to me under date of November 8, 1938, in these terms:
At the annual meeting of the Canadian chamber of agriculture, held at Winnipeg, October 28 and 29, Mr. H. H. Hannam of Toronto, vice president of the chamber, together with the secretary, were appointed a committee to present to you certain resolutions passed at this meeting, dealing with the subject of marketing legislation.
I do not think it is necessary to read the remainder of the letter; that one paragraph indicates the desire of the committee to meet me and present resolutions. What I am mostly concerned with is the resolutions themselves. The resolutions as presented at a later date read:
1.	That we recommend to each provincial organization (excepting British Columbia) that they press for legislation in their respective provinces on the lines of the British Columbia Marketing Act.
2.	That the Canadian chamber of agriculture urge upon the dominion government necessity for the immediate passage of a compulsory marketing act to deal with interprovincial and export trade.
I am going to read a further resolution which was brought along with this, because of its relationship to another question which is being dealt with at the present time and which these people thought at that time could be dealt with satisfactorily under legislation of this kind. I shall not read the "whereases"; they have to do with butter and the surpluses of butter which then existed. If one were to read all the "whereases" one would find that they were outlining a situation in which, although the price is on a different level, the difficulties related to the
8, 1949	2473
Agricultural Products Marketing Act price were very much the same as the difficulties we are discussing at the moment.
The active part of the resolution reads like this:
Therefore be it resolved we request the dominion government to pass legislation which will permit the producers of Canada to set up a board for the purpose of regulating the export of dairy products so that the producers' price may be more evenly maintained, and so that the consumers' price may not be in jeopardy by extreme seasonal fluctuation;
And it is further resolved that the industry will assume the cost of financing the operation of such a board, for which purpose we petition the government to pass the necessary legislation or regulations giving such board power to obtain necessary funds from the industry either through an equitable levy on the entire production, or a service fee, or licensing fee based on the volume of production in each plant, or through any other form of revenue from the industry which can be permitted and approved by the government.
Let me repeat that these three resolutions were brought down at the one time. I read the last one in order to refer to something which took place in this house and in the country at the time the Natural Products Marketing Act of 1934 was under discussion. I understand that the strongest objection to the passing of the Natural Products Marketing Act, made by those who were opposed to it in principle, was to the effect that under our system of government it had been customary to give taxing powers to people living within prescribed areas. In other words, we give taxing powers to provinces; the provinces, in turn, give taxing powers to municipalities, and then the municipalities or counties may be divided up into townships. An act to provide for the marketing or the promotion, control and regulation of the marketing of natural products in interprovincial trade in Canada and in export trade.

His Majesty, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate and House of Commons of Canada, enacts as follows:
Short Title
1.	This act may be cited as the Natural Products Marketing Act.
Purpose and Intent
2.	The purpose and intent of this act is to provide for the marketing and the promotion, control and regulation, or the prohibition, of the marketing in any or all respects of natural products in interprovincial trade in Canada and in export trade.
Powers
3.	Whenever under any law of a province any board or agency has been established to market, or promote, control, regulate or prohibit, the marketing of any natural product, the governor in council may confer upon such board or agency authority to exercise in respect to interprovincial trade or export trade in such product such powers similar to all or any of the powers provided by or under such provincial law, as may be within the legislative authority of the parliament of Canada, and may vary or retract such powers.
4.	The governor in council may make such regulations as may be necessary for the efficient enforcement and operation of this act, and for carrying out the provisions thereof, according to their true intent and meaning.
Offences
5.	Every person who fails to comply with any regulation of the governor in council, or with any order, rule, or regulation made by any such board or agency pursuant to the authority conferred under this act, shall be guilty of an offence and punishable on summary conviction with a fine of not less than twenty-five dollars and not more than five hundred dollars, or to imprisonment not exceeding three months, or to both fine and imprisonment.
That is the entire bill as submitted to us by the federation as a model bill when they presented their request for legislation to us. We replied that, for the duration of the war, any boards that were going to be set up for that purpose would be set up by the government. Those boards would take delivery of the product and market it wherever it could be marketed, more particularly in Great Britain.
When the war was over the Canadian Federation of Agriculture returned and requested once again that we put this legislation upon the statute books. At that time we stated we were still dealing directly with government boards in Great Britain under agreements. In order to set the minister's mind at rest, Mr. Speaker, as to the position of the official opposition, the Progressive Conservative party, I may tell him at the outset that we are in accord with the principle of this bill and with the objects which the bill seeks to accomplish, namely, the extension to provincial marketing boards of marketing powers with respect to interprovincial and export trade.
We feel, however, that there are certain aspects of the bill with regard to which we must have reservations; those of course we can discuss more fully in committee. There are certain matters with respect to marketing policy which I think it is important to bring to the attention of the house and the country at this time. The first remark I would make in that connection is that the very history given this afternoon by the minister of the efforts made in the past to attain a satisfactory dominion marketing act, and of the many requests made to the present federal government for the enactment of such an act, raises the question as to why it is being done in this form at this time in this great hurry. The answer of course is quite plain to everybody on both sides of the house and throughout the country. The answer is that, so far as the present government is concerned, this is a mere death-bed repentance.
I use those words advisedly, Mr. Speaker. It is a death-bed repentance because, amongst other things, it is done to save a dying government. It is too late, however, to save the present government from the consequences of their maladministration in the field of agriculture generally, and particularly is it too late to save them from the consequences of their repeated denials in the past to organized agriculture of a satisfactory federal marketing act. The minister gave us an historical outline of marketing legislation which, as a matter of fact, has certain factual gaps in it which I should like to fill in in a moment. But he gave us answers to what he said was the question as to why this sort of legislation had not been introduced before.
He said that the reason it was being introduced now was that since the war, since the request put forward by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture in 1947, we have eliminated much of the intergovernmental trading. He said there is not so much marketing through government boards since that time. That is one reason he gave why we can now introduce a marketing act. Of course there is another reason. The main reason that he is now introducing a marketing act is that since that time he is confronted with an election. That is obviously the reason why this act is now being introduced.

The situation is little different in 1949 from what it was in 1947 or in 1948. In 1947 I think there were five intergovernmental contracts as between this government and the United Kingdom-only five commodities subject to contracts. In 1948 that same situation prevailed. Now I think we have only four. But really there is little difference as between the two years. So the reason is quite obvious.
But however that may be, as I have said we are in accord with the principle of this legislation. In fact we have been urging for some fifteen or twenty years that such legislation should be enacted. It has been one of the fundamental principles of this party with respect to its agricultural program.
Hon. members will recall-those who are acquainted with this subject-that there were certain omissions from the minister's historical review of marketing legislation. Canadian agriculture has always found itself in a peculiar position with respect to marketing. We have a vast production and a limited domestic market. Our markets are limited both in respect to the province in which the production took place and with respect to export trade. Let me give just two examples. In British Columbia we produce far more apples than it is possible for us to consume domestically. Therefore the apple growers in British Columbia are faced with the problem with respect to exporting their apples to other markets and to other provinces.
In the same way in Canada, on a national scale, we produce more grain than we can possibly consume. Hence we are faced with a national export marketing problem. Whether it be on the provincial or on the dominion scale, export marketing has always been of special concern to Canadian agriculture. So we find a long history of struggle in Canada to obtain marketing legislation which would enable our growers to deal with that peculiar situation.
The first concrete attempt to deal with that situation was probably the Produce Marketing Act which was enacted in British Columbia as far back as 1927. This was an act which applied to tree fruits, but it was ruled to be ultra vires on appeal to the privy council, in a decision handed down in 1931. It was ruled to be ultra vires for the reason that, although it was enacted by a provincial legislature, it sought to give power to a provincial board over interprovincial and export trade. So unfortunately, under the constitutional position under which this country lives, the act was not within the competence of the legislature of the province.
The next attempt was again in British Columbia, and was the Dairy Products Sales

Agricultural Products Marketing Act Adjustment Act, passed in that province in 1929. That act in turn was held to be ultra vires of the provincial legislature by the privy council on an appeal in 1932. The grounds for that decision were that the act in effect imposed an indirect tax, and that the powers of indirect taxation were not given to the provinces under the constitution, and that therefore this particular act was not within the competence of the provincial legislature.
It then became obvious that the only people who could deal satisfactorily with this question of marketing were the federal government, or possibly a combination of the provincial and federal legislatures; and those who were interested in marketing turned to the federal parliament for a solution of their problem. The result was the passage of the Natural Products Marketing Act in 1934 under the administration of the late Viscount Bennett. This act provided for the setting up of dominion marketing boards and the introduction of marketing schemes with respect to individual products. It was based upon British marketing legislation, which in turn was based upon Australian marketing schemes. At approximately the same time, or I should say immediately after the federal legislation was passed, British Columbia passed complementary legislation, under which three marketing schemes were set up, schemes having to do with tree fruits, vegetables and dairy products. The attempt in British Columbia was to enable these boards to draw their powers from either the provincial act or the federal act. It was hoped that finally an act had been passed which was intra vires.
You will remember, Mr. Speaker, the violent opposition to the dominion Natural Products Marketing Act in this house in 1934, when the opposition, the party which now forms the government, sought by every means in its power to prevent that act from becoming law. You will remember also that after they became the government, instead of repealing the act, they took the rather less direct course of submitting it to the courts for a decision as to whether or not it was intra vires of the federal parliament. A decision was given in 1937, and that was appealed to the privy council, which held that the dominion Natural Products Marketing Act was not within the legislative competence of the federal government, mainly, as I recall, on the ground that it interfered with trade within the provinces, which was a matter reserved to the competence of the provincial legislatures.
That decision was given in 1937, and so again the attempt to set up an over-all marketing scheme for the dominion came to naught. But we now have it established-we
2478	HOUSE OF
Agricultural Products Marketing Act had it established in the next year 1938, for the first time-that an act passed within a province is within the legislative competence of the provinces, because in 1938, a year after the dominion's act was declared ultra vires, the complementary legislation which had been passed by British Columbia was appealed to the courts, and it was held by the privy council to be a valid act and within the competence of the legislature of British Columbia.
Therefore after eleven years of attempting, with one form of act or another, to find a valid scheme, we had in 1938 the first decision that a provincial marketing act was valid. Almost immediately afterwards the provinces of Ontario and New Brunswick passed acts similar to that of British Columbia, followed by Saskatchewan and Nova Scotia, and by virtually every other province since that time.
I have given a short factual history of the development of these schemes. It will be obvious, Mr. Speaker, that even though the provincial schemes were valid-and it should be observed that nearly all of them are based upon the general outline of the British Columbia scheme-still they are subject to one great weakness. The powers of the marketing boards set up under those schemes can extend only to trade within the provinces. Any other powers which they have can be derived only from a contractual relation between the marketing board and the agencies on which they rely to sell their products. But there can be no legislative sanction by one province for the control of its products in another; no British Columbia act can provide, let us say, for control by the British Columbia board of the marketing of its products within another province in Canada. The only way in which that can be controlled is by some form of contractual relation. That is the weakness which has beset marketing efforts in Canada up to the present. The provincial marketing schemes have no legislative authority outside their own provinces.
I should now like to turn for a moment to the desire of the producers of Canada for satisfactory marketing legislation. Their desire has been to have legislation which would enable the producers of agricultural goods to control the marketing of their own produce. They have found that they must have some scheme to enable them to organize so that they will be able to bargain on a basis of equality with those who sell their products, so that they will be able to bargain on a basis of equality with those with whom they must deal.


Marketing schemes are not set up, as has been so often alleged, in order to exploit consumers. If one thinks of this problem at all it becomes obvious that a large number of farmers, dealing with perishable commodities, are simply not in a position to bargain on a basis of equality so long as they are a number of unorganized individuals, and that they can only control their own destinies in any real sense of the word when they become organized, and when they are able to control all aspects of their own production and marketing.
In this respect I should like to refer to the words of the president of perhaps the most successful of these marketing agencies, namely, Mr. A. K. Loyd, president of British Columbia Tree Fruits Limited, which is the single selling agency for all the tree fruits in British Columbia. Mr. Loyd, speaking before the Washington state horticultural association, had this to say about marketing schemes:
It has never been a principle endorsed by the growers' selling agency that it is possible to obtain artificial prices for the growers. The law of supply and demand has governed from time immemorial, and will continue to do so indefinitely. All that the selling agency set out to do was to return to the pockets of the grower as much as possible of whatever the market was able to pay.
I think it is worth repeating, since one-desk selling has too often been represented as an attempt to establish artificial price levels. It is merely an attempt to return to the producers as much as possible of the market price, whatever that may be.
That attempt has been successful in nearly every province in Canada in so far as control of production and marketing of the commodity in trade within the province was concerned; and the most noteworthy feature of these schemes is that control is given to the producers. They are producers' boards. They are controlled by the growers, and I have never heard any suggestion, particularly in so far as the tree fruits industry is concerned, that there is outside interference, or that the thing is not so run as to have in mind the interest of the growers at every stage of the proceedings. The desire, then, of organized agriculture has been to extend this same principle of producer control to interprovincial and export trade. That has been the request of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture referred to earlier this afternoon by the minister, and I feel bound to say that it has been the request of the official opposition, and has been the stand of this party for many years.
We have found however from this government that just the opposite was the tendency. I would remind you, Mr. Speaker, of the proceedings in 1947 when the Agricultural Products Act was first before the house. Speaking for the official opposition the then member for Yale, the Hon. Grote Stirling,

took exception to that bill because he said it was not a marketing act, but that it was a control act. Instead of the power to control the production and marketing of agricultural commodities being given to producers and producer boards, those powers were given to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner). He has exclusive power; he has the power to set prices, the power to requisition products, the power to compel delivery. In fact there is no suggestion of giving power to producers. It is a derogation from the powers otherwise held by producer boards.
The hon. member at that time introduced an amendment to that measure for the reasons set out at page 1372 of Hansard for 1947.
We are not in accord with the principle behind this bill-
He was referring to the Agricultural Products Act. There has been some confusion, Mr. Speaker, because the titles of these two measures are very similar. The one of which Mr. Stirling was speaking at that time was called the Agricultural Products Act. As I have said, it was a control act. The bill we are now discussing is called the Agricultural Products Marketing Act, and it is a true marketing act.
Speaking of the Agricultural Products Act, Mr. Stirling said in 1947:
We are not in accord with the principle behind this bill, because we believe that there should be recognition by the government of the existing boards, and it should be so stated in the bill. I intend to make that the subject of an amendment which I propose to move, seconded by the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Charlton), and which I shall now read. It is as follows:
"That the said bill be not now read the second time, but that it be resolved that an Agricultural Products Act should be based on the principle that producer boards, set up under provincial marketing acts, where such boards exist, or as they may from time to time come into existence, be used for the purposes of such Agricultural Products Act, instead of commodity boards established by the minister under section four of the said bill."
That amendment was not accepted, but was ruled out of order. As I recall it, another similar amendment on second reading was voted down. So the Agricultural Products Act, in its present form a control act, has continued in force, and was renewed by the House of Commons less than a month ago.
I do not intend to refer to the debates which have taken place earlier this session, but I believe I am in order when I say that there is a conflict in principle between the Agricultural Products Act passed in 1947 and extended earlier this session, and the bill now before the house. One was a control act giving absolute power over agricultural commodities to the minister. The bill now before us gives power to the boards, or perhaps to be more specific it is a measure extending the
8, 1949	2479
Agricultural Products Marketing Act powers of the provincial boards to the sphere of interprovincial and export trade.
I said then, and I repeat, that the proper course to have taken would have been to drop the earlier bill, and to proceed with this one, which should have been passed first. Under this bill there can be orderly regulation of the marketing of agricultural products; under the bill now before us the situation desired by organized agriculture is at last brought into effect, that is that the producer boards are given control over their own activities.
In fact I find it difficult to know how those who on the one hand voted in favour of giving control to the Minister of Agriculture now find that they can reverse themselves and say that we should give control to the producer boards. I find it difficult to know how they can go through that contortion. I am glad to believe that they are going to be able to do so because, from what I understand, both the parties which supported the earlier bill, which was a control measure and one that took control away from the producer boards, are now about to support the present bill which has to do with marketing and' gives power to the provincial boards. I repeat that I am unable to understand their mental gymnastics, but I am glad to find! that they are able to adopt that procedure. We hope that as the result this bill will become law.
I believe there is some question as to the constitutional difficulty which has always beset attempts to introduce dominion marketing legislation: I understand the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) will speak in this connection, and when he does I hope he will confirm my impression. It is my view that this bill meets the constitutional difficulty because it will have to be based upon co-operation between the provinces. It does not seek to set up a board which will have jurisdiction over trade within a province. It empowers existing boards to control the marketing of their commodities in interprovincial and export trade. As I see it, therefore, the working of this measure will have to be based upon co-operation between the provinces and between the various provincial boards in existence. I should hope-and I think it is logical so to hope-that as the working out of this marketing scheme progresses, agricultural producers may find it possible to set up for themselves their own over-all marketing scheme, if such is found necessary.
However, as I have said, I believe this is a matter which is properly left to organized agriculture. They now have the basis in their provincial boards. They have the practical experience, as a result of the-

Mr. Speaker, the members of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation welcome this bill. I had intended to speak at some length on it but as we are desirous of having it passed before the Easter recess I shall be brief in my remarks. First I want to point out that we welcome this bill because the producers of this country have fought for many years to have legislation of this kind in order that they might have some assurance that they would get a fair price for what they produced. I feel I can speak with some authority because I have been a producer of farm products for the last twenty years and have gone through the process of having my returns stolen on the speculative market.
I feel that this bill proposed by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) offers some solution for our problem. While it provides for the setting up of provincial boards which may be able to deal with the situation to the satisfaction of some producers, yet I feel that there may be danger in that the results which most of us would like to see may not be achieved. I have a letter dated April 4 from the Saskatchewan poultry board. If I had the time I would like to read into the record the submissions which have been made to the government of Canada by the Canadian poultry industry. While they support an act such as the one proposed, at the same time they point out some of the difficulties.
I think their difficulties are somewhat similar to those faced by the producers of coarse grains and other farm products. The farmers and producers of Canada do not want to see a situation develop where when we have a surplus of a few tubfuls of butter, that will set the price of butter; where when we have a few extra steers, that will set the price of livestock products; similarly, where when we have a few extra bushels of coarse grains, that will set the price for coarse grains. Rather they feel that there should be adequate legislation to meet the needs of agriculture in this country.
Under the proposed bill we will be able to set up provincial boards. The submissions made by the Saskatchewan poultry board and those made on behalf of the poultry industry of Canada indicate that the contracts which were obtained during the war encouraged the development of the poultry industry until it had increased about 25 per cent. The industry is now facing a lack of markets. They recommend that in order to handle surpluses there should be set up

a central selling agency which could market these surpluses without deranging the market.
I think the minister will realize that it is necessary to have agricultural products channeled from the producer to the consumer without deranging the market.
I listened with some interest to the remarks of the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton). While I think he did a good job as a young lawyer in putting forward the case of the Progressive Conservative party, it seemed to me that he did not quite understand the full intent of this bill. Certainly the boards which will be set up will be compulsory in character. Subsection (2) of section 2 of the bill reads:
The governor in council may by order revoke any authority granted under subsection one.
That gives the governor in council complete jurisdiction over the board. Those producing poultry are satisfied with this bill. The hon. member for Yale (Mr. Jones) was unable to be here today because he had made other arrangements, but on his behalf I should like to refer to a letter which he received from the British Columbia interior vegetable marketing board suggesting that they were in full support of this bill. On behalf of the hon. member for Yale may I say that he is in full support of the bill. On February 4 he made an excellent speech in this house recommending that such a bill be brought in at this session so that the fruit growers of British Columbia would have proper marketing facilities for their products.
I should like to refer now to coarse grains. About eighteen months ago Bill No. 135 was introduced into this house to bring coarse grains under the Canadian wheat board. That act was never proclaimed because the provinces of Manitoba and Alberta failed to pass the complementary legislation which would have made that act operative. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) has refused to proclaim the act until those two provinces have passed enabling legislation. Last year when the Minister of Agriculture was going through the west he indicated that provincial boards could be set up under that act to handle coarse grains adequately. He failed to tell us, however, how the provincial boards which may be set up under this act would handle the situation. That is one of the difficulties that I see in the act. It does not provide definitely for anything. It is merely a provisional act to allow the provinces to set up their own agricultural marketing boards.
My understanding is that the terminal grain elevators, for example, are what are termed works to the general advantage of Canada. I fail to see how provincial boards could

Agricultural Products Marketing Act operate without jurisdiction over those elevators. Then there is the matter of railway cars. I cannot see how the provinces can adequately handle the- channeling of their grain over the railroads without having control of railway cars. Then there are the storage facilities that would be necessary at the lakehead, a matter which is again outside the jurisdiction of the provinces. If we set up provincial marketing boards merely to handle our coarse grains, rather than having them come under the wheat board, I cannot see how it can be really satisfactory, because of necessity we must export a lot of our coarse grains, as well as our wheat. Moreover, as I have said since I have come into the house, I believe-and this is a part of our C.C.F. program-that unless we can plan nationally for our agricultural producers then we are certain to run into a lot of difficulties. I would have preferred to have a more comprehensive act with proper clauses in it so that we would know exactly where we stand. It seems to me that under the proposed measure we will still have a conglomeration of acts under which our farm commodities will be marketed, and we will always be running into many difficulties.
I should like to say in conclusion, however, that I support the bill. As farmers, as agricultural producers, we have been fighting for something in the way of a national marketing act comprehensive enough to give justice to the primary producers. When we go into committee I shall ask the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) to tell us if it is proposed that the provinces must market coarse grains rather than bring them under the federal wheat board. I want to know how it is proposed to be done.

This measure is in the nature of enabling legislation. Apparently the officers of the Department of Justice take the view, and I think correctly so, that matters of export trade and interprovincial trade come within federal jurisdiction. The object of the bill is to pass along to the provinces a portion of jurisdiction which properly belongs to the

Agricultural Products Marketing Act federal government. What will happen? When this legislation passes, I presume every province which has a marketing act-we have one in New Brunswick, and I think all the maritime provinces have marketing acts- will endeavour to take advantage of it.
Our problem is the marketing of our huge crops of potatoes in outside markets, and in central Canada. The difficulty applies mostly to New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, and to some extent Nova Scotia. We export considerable quantities to South America and Central America. The trouble has been that in past years there have been cutthroat practices amongst the different dealers in the maritime provinces. I am sure as far as New Brunswick is concerned that is so. I have here a letter from the minister of agriculture of New Brunswick which corroborates that statement. In New Brunswick the producers have never been able to get together to set a price. They have been underselling one another in these markets. To a large extent that has been the cause of a great many of our difficulties. Let us assume that under this legislation the New Brunswick government proceeds to set a minimum price at New Brunswick seaports for the export of our potatoes, because what is exported through the seaports is mostly seed potatoes to South America and Central America. Suppose they set a price of $2 per 100 pounds at Saint John, and Prince Edward Island sets a price of $1.90, Nova Scotia a price of $2.10 and Quebec a price of $2.20. What will be the outcome? We will have to face the same unfair competition that we have been facing as between individual exporters.
Countries which are purchasing will purchase where the prices are lower unless these provincial. boards can get together all across Canada and agree on a minimum price for the export of their farm products, or agree on a minimum price for products moving from one province to the other. Unless we can get them to agree on that I am afraid that this legislation will not be very helpful.
I am not closely in touch with the federation of agriculture, and therefore I am not in a position to say whether or not they have any views on this matter. The minister will know that. I agree with the hon. member who has just taken his seat, in that I feel the present legislation is not sufficient. Permanent legislation, such as the Agricultural Prices Support Act, should be enacted. The member for Restigouche-Madawaska (Mr. Michaud) had something to say about the potato growers of his province costing Canada a large sum of money. I feel that other industries in addition to agriculture are continuously costing the people of Canada a great deal of money. Because agriculture is of prime importance to the Canadian family it should not be treated as an orphan when it comes to prices and working conditions. I feel it is time legislation was enacted which would put agriculture on an equal footing with the other industries in this country. Until we have a prosperous agriculture we certainly cannot have a prosperous Canada.

Agricultural Products Marketing Act One of the best authorities in Canada, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), is on record as stating that the farmers have received poor prices during the war. I am going to quote from the Ottawa Journal of February 10 something the minister had to say to a farmers' organization in Ontario. The article is headed, "War Sacrifices of Farmers Entitle Them to Fair Prices."
Canadian farmers were "entitled now" to prices which would justify their wartime sacrifices, Agriculture Minister Gardiner said last night. He was speaking to the annual meeting of the Ontario Concentrated Milk Producers Association at the Chateau Laurier. More than 150 delegates are attending the two-day session, the largest in several years.
"Because there have been declines in the United States, people here are suggesting that food prices should drop to that level, forgetting that prices there rose during the war to a peak never experienced here."
The whole idea in preventing high food prices in Canada during wartime was to allow a "leveling out" afterwards, Mr. Gardiner remarked.
He was "inclined to agree" with the popular statement that consumers did not appreciate what farmers did during the war in keeping the cost of food down. Mr. Gardiner said he was "surprised that farmers had not been able to sell that idea fully."
To reduce the cost of food would mean "bringing down returns to farmers."
"People are inclined to forget that farmers, and dairy farmers in particular, were asked to hold their hand on prices during the war-at a time when they might have charged almost what they wanted."
I agree wholeheartedly with the minister in that statement. The farmer has had comparatively slight increases in the prices of the products he has to sell.
We find that the cost of production has risen to a high level. To take one instance alone, the cost of farm machinery before the war was in excess of what it should have been: on the figures put out lately by the Massey-Harris Company we find that the price of farm machinery has increased by 43-9 per cent. Anyone who takes the trouble to figure out the price of agricultural products will find that it has not kept pace with the cost of production.
Before getting away from that part of my argument I should like to state that during the 1946-47 crop year, according to figures brought down in the house in my name, the farmers of the prairie provinces have lost no less than eighty-six cents a bushel on the wheat sold to the British government in 1946; and in 1947 there is an apparent loss of $1.22.
I am not saying that is the final amount, but the apparent figures show that amount. In addition to that, it is a well-known fact that the prices of coarse grains that were fed here in Canada, and of other products sold to Britain, were based on the price of wheat in the agreement.
I am like other members who have spoken before me. I do not want to be accused of


holding up this bill. We also, after waiting for so many years, want to see this bill passed tonight if that is possible. In order to help the minister and the government, I should like to place on record the Social Credit agricultural and primary producer policy.
(a)	A home market supplied with sufficient purchasing power to enable the people to buy the goods which they require for their use.
(b)	Adequate and low cost credit facilities through agencies especially acquainted with agricultural and marketing conditions.
(c)	Floor prices sufficient to cover the average production costs and to give farm producers a net return for their services, bearing a fair relationship to that secured by citizens engaged in industrial production and distribution.
(d)	Grain marketing-[DOT]
(1)	Revision of the Canadian Wheat Board Act so that the board shall be an agency operating primarily for the benefit of, and in the interests of, grain producers.
(2)	That the Canadian wheat board market all commercial wheat.
(3)	Support long-term international wheat agreements to conform with the policy set out above.
(e)	Continuation of the operation of the Agricultural Prices Support Act as permanent legislation.
(f)	Adequate producer representation on all boards and agencies having control over farm products.
(g)	Setting up of federal legislation to provide for voluntary crop insurance.
To deal for a moment with each of those items, in connection with (a) I should like to refer the minister and the government to the analysis made by Professor Hope in dealing with the ability to supply purchasing power so that all the people of Canada could at least have enough to eat. Professor Hope's name is well known in this house, and his record for doing good work in Saskatchewan and at the present time for the Canadian Federation of Agriculture is I believe recognized all across this country.
As to (b), we have at the present time the Canadian farm loan board and the Agricultural Credit Act administration. These two agencies are in my opinion charging too high a rate of interest, because there is no need in the world to have a rate of four and one-half per cent and five per cent interest charged on loans to farmers. If the farmers are not a good risk, I believe it is the duty and the business of the government to see that an agricultural policy is put into effect that will make our farmers good risks like those in other lines of business in the country.
As to (c) I do not think it is necessary for me to repeat our argument, because we have on many occasions stressed the need and given sufficient reasons for fair prices. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), in the statement I quoted a little while ago, also bears out this argument.
As to (d) (1), we feel that the Canadian wheat board should sell grain for the highest prices that it will bring under our present conditions, and that it should not be used as

an agency to take from the producers and give to the consumers out of the producers' funds. If the government finds it necessary and desirable to pay a bonus, I believe that bonus should come out of the consolidated revenue fund of this country. The producers of this country should not be asked to subsidize other producers who are feeding part of their grain. That procedure is particularly undesirable because of the policy that has been pursued in connection with the sale of our grain and other products in the past.
As to (d) (2), under present circumstances I believe that is the only way we shall get the best service and the best price for our grain; because if we are to have a number of individual sellers and just two or three purchasers, we shall come out on the wrong end of the deal.
As to (d) (3), I think we made our stand on that question known when the international wheat agreement was introduced the other day. I shall have more to say when that agreement is brought in for ratification.
As to (e), my friend across the way who just finished speaking gave some reasons, and many other reasons have been advanced on this side of the house why that legislation should be continued as a permanent measure.
As to (f), I think anybody taking a realistic view of the marketing of farm products, or of any other products for that matter, will see the necessity for having people on the selling board-not on the advisory boards but on the selling board-who understand the position and have at heart the interests of those particularly concerned.
As to (g), that has been asked for by organizations for a number of years. I understand that system is working satisfactorily in the United States, that it is becoming more and more effective, and that more and more farmers are going in under it. That of course is a voluntary organization. I hope this agricultural and primary producer policy of this organization will help the government to set up a much better agricultural policy for Canadian farmers and to make Canada a prosperous country all through.

It is not my
intention to delay the house for any length of time because I realize that everybody is anxious to get this matter through. I have listened with much interest to the speeches which have been made. I was deeply interested in the remarks of the last speaker, but I must say that I was disappointed when he mentioned the men from British Columbia who had done so much to promote this marketing legislation. He did not mention the name of one man who I know has done as much as if not more than any other member in this house to promote marketing acts. I refer to Hon. Grote Stirling. I am sure that the hon. member must have forgotten him, because he mentioned another Mr. Stirling, but he did not mention Grote Stirling, the former member. In the time that I have been in the house I remember that Mr. Esling, who also represented the riding which the present member represents, was a strong advocate of marketing acts.
I had intended to make extensive remarks this afternoon, but unfortunately the time is short, and I shall say what I have to say in a few minutes. At the outset I want to assure the house that I am in entire agreement with the principle of this bill, but I also want to assure the house that I agree with the remarks that were made by my colleague, the hon. member for Restigouche-Madawaska (Mr. Michaud), to the effect that this bill does not seem to meet the requirements of the maritime provinces, and particularly the potato growers of New Brunswick.
When we speak of the necessity of legislation of this kind it is only necessary to point out the chaotic condition of potato marketing in New Brunswick to realize that some federal act and a co-ordinate provincial act is necessary. As has been stated before, this year we had a surplus crop of potatoes. We sold a considerable quantity in the United States market, and then under an embargo our market in the United States was cut off almost immediately.
As the minister knows, we were allowed to sell seed potatoes in the United States, and again the marketing of seed potatoes was interfered with by many of the large exporters of seed potatoes in the province selling seed potatoes for table use. The United States complained of this type of sale, which has also added to the chaotic condition of the potato market in New Brunswick.
In former years we used to sell to the Cuban market. That market was lost to us. We sold to the South American market, and again, as the hon. member for Restigouche-Madawaska said, there was competition between potato dealers in Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick. Those in New

Brunswick were in competition with potato dealers in Nova Scotia, and those in Nova Scotia were in competition with dealers in Quebec. The result was that the whole market for this product, which means so much to the economy of our province, was chaotic. I sincerely hope that the minister will explain to us how some order can be brought out of the present condition.
As I said when I rose, it is not my intention to make any extended remarks. I do hope however that this marketing measure can be made workable in our maritime provinces. What applies to potatoes also applies to apples to a lesser degree. I was amazed the other day to hear the minister say that in the government's decision to cut down apple trees in Nova Scotia they were uprooting and cutting down trees in one year in numbers which they had expected to dispose of in three years. He said that was a proper procedure, because they would not be bothered with the sale of the apples from fruit trees after they had been cut down.
That is not the type of marketing legislation we want for our produce from the maritime provinces. We do not want to cut down our apple trees so as to dispose of the apples which would be produced. We do not wish to have to depend upon a smaller acreage in potatoes, because there is a great demand for potatoes, if not in this country then certainly in other parts of the world.
I trust that through this measure the minister will be able to work out something which would be satisfactory in connection with the marketing of potatoes from New Brunswick, as well as the marketing of our other farm products.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR MARKETING IN INTERPROVINCIAL AND EXPORT TRADE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is an important piece of legislation, and thus far we have discussed it for only two hours. In doing the nation's business I believe we should not hurry at this point, because the present measure brings into focus the whole question of the best manner in which to dispose of our agricultural products.
A great deal has been said in that respect both in the house and in other places during the last twenty-five years. We of the C.C.F. have always taken the position that trade or marketing is essentially an intelligent exchange of goods, and that to the extent any agency assists in making that intelligent exchange of goods more efficient or easier, such agency is good.
That is why we have opposed speculative marketing as a marketing method. We believe speculation does not add anything to the value of goods exchanged, and that essentially it adds to the cost of exchanging those goods for other goods or services. That is
Agricultural Products Marketing Act why in the house we have always taken the strong position of doing away with speculative interests which enter into the exchange of goods, whether in our domestic markets or our export trade.
I was keenly interested in something that was said this afternoon about death-bed repentance. I am glad that expression was used, because I think it is time some points were cleared up so far as this matter of repentance is concerned. We of the C.C.F. are in the happy position of having no repentance to make, because we have taken the stand consistently for orderly marketing of agricultural products. However, when members of the Progressive Conservative party sitting to my right speak about deathbed repentance they are taking a text which is likely to backfire.
As I listened to the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) I could not help remembering that it was only on March 25 that the hon. member for Calgary East (Mr. Harkness), one of the members of his party, was asked to state whether he believed in the orderly marketing of farm products. The hon. member replied that he did not care who handled his products or how much gambling was done on his grain, provided he received a better price as a result. He expressed the philosophy of the party to which he belongs.
In order to make sure that he was speaking seriously I asked him specifically at the time whether he was voicing his own opinion or that of his party, and he replied in these words:
I am giving, as I always do, my personal opinions. But I think I am expressing fairly well the opinions of a majority of the people in this party.
Let me say to him that he certainly was not expressing the opinion of the majority of the people of the prairie provinces. It is this belief, or this weakness as a result of which people believe that gambling can add something to the value of their product, which keeps the speculative markets alive, and which keeps gambling dens such as the Winnipeg grain exchange operating for their own profit and to the detriment of both producers and consumers.
It is because there are farmers-if the hon. member can so describe himself, in the full sense-who think that by some magic means or by being smarter than the gamblers on the grain exchange they can get a higher price than is received by their neighbours for their products, and that they can use the labour of other farmers to bring them a better return for their own produce, that these naive people place themselves in a position where the grain exchange and other speculative interests are making a good living from the hides of those

While he spoke I thought of discussions which took place in this house in 1935 with respect to marketing. While I was not here at the time, I recall that the Bennett administration introduced a marketing act to which reference has been made this afternoon. Under the marketing act there is power in these boards to create criminal offences, not offences for which the penalty is a fine of $10 for the first offence and $20 for the second, but a fine of $25 and not more than $500, or imprisonment for three months, or both fine and imprisonment.

speechtext:
No; to be fair to Russia I do not think you could get anyone to put through such legislation as that in Russia now.
At that time it was the opinion of the Liberals that the Bennett administration was even more dictatorial than communist Russia. To what were they objecting? The objection on the part of the Liberal opposition was to the principle of compulsion behind the marketing act. Under the terms of that act the producers were not to be allowed to dispose of their products, boards would be set up which would have the power to make regulations under which the products would be sold. Every time that legislation of that kind has been brought in by the present administration during the last four years we heard the same argument against it from the Progressive Conservative opposition. Obviously they are both right or they are both wrong. They have used the same criticism against each other and have cancelled out each other's criticism. I am glad that the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) is able to stand up in his place today and say that the party with which he is associated is wholeheartedly behind the principle of this bill.
As a matter of fact, about all that there is to support in this bill is the principle behind it. There is very little else in it but the principle of orderly marketing. As it stands now, the terms of the bill are not clear enough nor effective enough actually to provide orderly marketing in either domestic or export trade. Basically the bill provides for the granting of power to boards set up under provincial legislation and extending their authority into interprovincial and export trade. That may work or it may not work, depending upon the circumstances under which the work is done.
One can easily appreciate the confusion that will be created if the marketing boards of various provinces were to attempt to sell products in such a way as not to result in a co-operative effort. It is the view of this party that this legislation should be changed in order to make it possible for the boards set up under provincial legislation to set up a central selling agency to act on behalf of all or a majority of the provinces in relation to world trade.

The hon. member for Restigouche-Mada-waska (Mr. Michaud) brought that out clearly in connection with the disposal of potatoes. He pointed out that this bill as it stands today would not be sufficient to cope with that problem, which has already become a big problem in his province and which may become a big problem in Prince Edward Island.
The C.C.F. has always urged that a comprehensive natural products marketing act should be introduced and if necessary submitted to the provinces for consultation. Such legislation should be broad and comprehensive enough to make it possible for farmers to dispose of their products and receive the greatest possible return for their labour. There should also be the minimum of speculation or profit-making because, as I have said before, profiteering or speculation does not add one iota to the value of the goods exchanged. That is the position we take today.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR MARKETING IN INTERPROVINCIAL AND EXPORT TRADE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a word in support of the principle of the bill. We consider that this is only an alternative to a real federal marketing act and we hope that some day this government will bring in such an act. The Canadian producers are facing a situation with regard to the exportable surpluses that exist. This situation is not going to be remedied by setting up internal or interprovincial boards, nor will it be remedied by provincial boards entering foreign fields.
Export trade is really a federal matter. Proper federal import and export boards should be set up. This is imperative if Canada is to escape the results of our export policy which existed in 1930. The minister will remember the prices that were obtained in Canada in 1932 for farm products. Oats were selling for as low as three or four cents per bushel; wheat was selling for as low as 19 cents per bushel; a farmer would bring in a dozen hogs and perhaps get $10. At that time it was difficult to exchange 20 or 30 dozen eggs for a pound of coffee. The Canadian people are not going to face that kind of thing again, especially when they know that in the world there are millions of hungry people.
There will have to be some change in the economy which in the past produced a situation where those who produced food for a hungry world were repaid for efficiently doing their job by having prices brought down so low that they did not cover the cost of production. Because they did their job they were faced with nothing but poverty and want, with the loss of their homes, with a mortgaged farm economy.
There will be a need, not only for agreements inside the country but for agreements
8, 1949
Agricultural Products Marketing Act in the international field. It will be necessary for the government to set up federal boards to deal with this matter so that when representatives meet at international conferences they can state in an authoritative way what surpluses will be available over a period of years. That cannot be done under a bill of this kind.
But since this bill goes along the road to some extent, since it lays down the basic principle that agreements can be made among the people inside the country and between provinces for the exchange of goods, we support it. But I want to make it abundantly clear that we do not look upon this bill as a solution of the problem which is facing Canada, and in a very real way.
I know that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) has received recommendations from egg producers and hog producers across Canada that there is a need for federal boards to handle the export of their surpluses. Canadian agricultural producers are alarmed over the surpluses that already exist in Canada. We do hope that the setting up of federal boards will be announced as a government policy in the near future because it will be too late when everything collapses.
One good point about this legislation is that it provides that boards operating provincially or interprovincially may arrange for the exchange of goods within the country, so that we will not have people living within a few hundred yards of granaries filled with wheat facing a condition of dire need. It is ridiculous to think of elevators being filled to the top with wheat and food products when children are facing hunger.
The establishment of export boards and the arrangement of international agreements through the federal government will mean that such organizations as the open market will not be permitted to function and make a very good living, as has been done in the past, from the fluctuation in prices between the fall and spring and from year to year. As a people living in a modern economy, it is going to become necessary for us to stop gambling in food, and to establish through international agreements the stability which is essential to the well-being and economy of both the producer and the consumer in any country. Stabilization of prices is going to become essential to the security of the people, and that means both producers and consumers.

" (2) The governor in council may by order grant authority to any two or more such provincial boards or agencies to form a central selling agency for the purposes of interprovincial and export trade. Such central selling agency shall have any or all powers like the powers exercisable by the provincial boards or agencies comprising the said central selling agency."

It seems to me that, unless there is some such provision in the act, you will have five, six or seven selling agencies set up by provincial boards which will not be able to co-operate in the disposal of their products, either in interprovincial or in export trade.
Therefore I believe that there should be a section in the act which will provide for the setting up of these central selling agencies. Perhaps that can be understood from the act now. I am not a lawyer. I do not know whether the sections now in the act provide for that. If they do not, I think we certainly should see to it that there is in it a clause which will provide for the setting up of central selling agencies. He said: I should like to have agreed that we go on with the agricultural act. I am afraid that little attention is going to be paid to the question of labour in this house; therefore I felt in honour bound to make an attempt to study the case of labour at this time. This kind of bill is not anything new to the house. In the industrial committee of the house in the last session this particular question of the voluntary and revocable check-off was dealt with. At that time the committee agreed to have it included in the bill. Unfortunately when it came to the house that particular clause was stricken out. The clause which now forms the bill before the house is exactly the same as the clause which the house struck from Bill No. 185 last year. The discussion on the bill at that particular time was extended. It comprises some six pages of Hansard, and it can be found starting at page 5369 of Hansard of June 17.
I do not think it is necessary to have much discussion on it, in view of the long discussion which took place on the previous occasion; but I want to say that this is something which the trade union movement of this country, irrespective of the congress concerned, is particularly interested in having incorporated in an act.
It is true that in many instances we do have the check-off as a result of collective bargaining, but there are innumerable instances, despite all the efforts at collective bargaining, where we have failed completely to secure the co-operation of an employer, even though his employees readily agree to have the deduction of dues.
As a result of negotiations we have frequently had the employees sign the authorization cards, and during the negotiations we have presented them to the employer, and informed him most courteously that these cards were an expression of the wishes of his employees. In the face of that he has still refused to agree to the check-off. It is to deal with employers of that particular kind that we of the trade union movement feel it is necessary to have a clause of this kind in the industrial relations law of the country.
As I estimate the amount and the kind of business that this house is going to do during this session, I cannot help coming to the conclusion that not much is to be done for the trade union movement and trade unionists

throughout the country. I had thought that amid the great amount of business that this house will do it could agree to this bill, if only as a gesture of good will to the trade union movement of this country.
There are already all kinds of deductions from the wages of employees. The government itself makes sure that by law it gets its deductions. There is a law to compel the deduction of income tax; there is a law to compel the deduction of unemployment insurance payments; there is even a law permitting garnisheeing of wages, all permissible by law. Outside of the law there are all kinds of other deductions, such as deductions for Red Cross, the community chests, numerous health plans and all kinds of social and recreational deductions. In fact I came across one particular group of employees who have no less than fourteen deductions from their wages. In the light of all these deductions, some by law and some not by law, the trade union movement now feels that the refusal to agree to having this voluntary revocable check-off made legal is a distinct discrimination against our trade union movement.
Many years ago when the late Earl Baldwin visited this country he addressed a very influential gathering at the university of Toronto. On that occasion he described the trade union movement of Great Britain as one of the cardinal institutions of the country. I believe the trade unions are a cardinal institution of Canada. I think the least that this house can do for this cardinal institution of the country is to agree that this bill, which is now before the house, shall be included as part of the labour law of Canada. Therefore I trust, Mr. Speaker, that the house will readily agree to this bill going forward.

maintopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  DEDUCTION OF UNION DUES
speechtext:
I should like to say a few words on this measure. The hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Williams), who has just taken his seat, began his remarks, I understand, by saying that this parliament would apparently not pay much attention to labour. My own experience in this house has been very short, but the hon. member's experience is even shorter than mine.
At the last session of parliament I had the pleasure of serving on the industrial relations committee of this house. It was certainly one of the most industrious, best attended and most interesting committees that I had anything to do with at the last session. As a result of the deliberations of that committee, and of the committee which sat throughout the previous session of parliament, the national labour code was enacted into law.
I do not pretend to be an expert on labour matters. My contributions to the labour committee were few, but I did find it an interesting thing to sit on that committee and

to hear expressions of opinion by hon. members who have had lifelong experience in the trade union movement and in union affairs in the old country, in the United States and in this country.
As I understand it, the basis of our system of labour legislation and our conception of the proper method of dealing with labour problems are, so far as possible to do it on the system of free collective bargaining between employers and employees. The whole plan of our national labour code is to set up the necessary machinery so that the employers and employees can meet, as closely as possible, on equal terms, and agree among themselves on the conditions of employment, wages and the other matters which are of supreme importance to both factions, the employers and labour. In so far as has been possible we have kept clear of any form of compulsion in our labour legislation. I believe that creates the very best atmosphere in which labour can meet industry, and secures from industry, from the employer, the greatest amount of co-operation and the best deal in respect of wage rates and conditions of employment.
This labour code, which was the achievement of the industrial relations committee during two sessions, was enacted only twelve months ago. It has not yet been in effect for a full year. I submit it is not reasonable to ask the house immediately to change a considered decision of both the committees which studied the provisions of this bill.

The one point about which I am most concerned, and the one which I believe should be driven home, is that this is supposed to be a national labour code. At least fifteen years ago every province in Canada, with the exception of the two central provinces, enacted labour codes and trade union acts of their own. In every one of those trade union acts we find this type of checkoff. That is the law of the provinces now. No province in Canada will accept this as a national code unless the provision we suggest is written in. If they did, it would be a backward step. The hon. member and I listened to Davie Grenfell the other day, an old friend of his and mine of many years' standing, when he spoke about the coal industry before the Canadian club in this city. Let me say to my hon. friend that they have not the check-off in South Wales, nor does the legislation in Great Britain contain the provisions that have been advocated on this side of the Atlantic. Perhaps it is that they have more sense, that they have a deeper appreciation of the fact that what governments can give they can take away. As I have explained before in this House of Commons, that is exemplified by what happened in Germany. At one time the German trade union movement was the most powerful in the world, notwithstanding the prominence of the trade union in Great Britain. Employers and employees went to the state to have regulations passed covering everything. When the revolution occurred they were not free citizens; they were simply servants of the state.
I have some knowledge of the Tolpuddle martyrs of Great Britain, some of whom are buried outside of London, Ontario. I have some knowledge of what trade unionism went through in Great Britain, the cradle of the trade union movement as we understand it in the world today. If the hon. member for Ontario will go back home among his constituents I think he will take the opinion of those simple souls-I am one myself-in their approach to this sort of problem.

Mr. Speaker, I am afraid I was a bit hasty before the supper recess in prematurely moving my motion for an instruction to the committee. I hope at this time that you may be able to find it in order. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Swift Current (Mr. Bentley):
That it be an instruction to the committee of the whole that they have power to amend Bill 82 by inserting therein immediately after section 2, subsection (1), the following new subsection (2):
"(2) The governor in council may by order grant authority to any two or more such provincial boards or agencies to form a central selling agency for the purposes of interprovincial and export trade. Such central selling agency shall have any or all powers like the powers exercisable by the provincial boards or agencies comprising the said central selling agency."
And by re-numbering the present subsection (2) of section 2 as subsection (3).
I move this instruction to the committee because I feel that the act, while it is good as far as it goes, does not go far enough. Under it provincial marketing boards will be set up in each of the provinces, and they will be authorized to enter into interprovincial and export trade. To do that they have to set up some sort of selling agency to sell their products interprovincially and in export markets. Let us take coarse grains and see what will happen in western Canada. There are three provinces there, and if their coarse grains were not marketed under the wheat board undoubtedly they would proceed under this act to set up provincial boards. What position would that put them in if there were three provincial boards, each selling coarse grains in the export market in competition with each other instead of in co-operation? You will have the same situation as far as honey or any other agricultural product is concerned. It will simply mean that every province will be setting up its own agency to sell the same products.
I see no reason why we should not give authority to these provincial boards under this act, when they are carrying on trade interprovincially and in export markets, to set up a central selling agency to act for those provinces in concert. It seems to me to be the sensible thing to do.

We brought him to Ottawa and had him work along with the officials of our own department in drafting legislation which, we were assured-that is as sure as one can be on matters of this kind- would be intra vires. As the minister concerned, I asked that the bill be drafted so that the authority which we had to give could be transferred to the agency or board that might be set up under provincial legislation to do this particular job.
In so far as I am able to understand English, that provision is made. This bill does not provide that the government must set up some particular form of board or particular form of organization. It does exactly what the farmers have requested. With regard to the marketing of oats and barley, to which reference has been made by the member for Melfort (Mr. Wright), it leaves the matter entirely in the hands of the producers. That is what they requested. When they were here last month they said they wanted a board which was a producers board. They were even critical of the present wheat board, stating it was not a producers board. This legislation makes it possible for them to have a producers board established by themselves without any interference on the part of the government.

. . . be the sole marketing agency of coarse grains and that any legislation giving the Canadian wheat board the same exclusive powers over the marketing of other grains as it now exercises over wheat shall be based on the principle that the Canadian wheat board shall be an agency operating for the benefit and the interest of grain producers with a duty to sell grain for the best available price whether in export or domestic markets.
