The question has been asked as to whether I am acquainted with the resolution which was passed at Saskatoon. I answer that question by saying that I was one of the committee of three of council that met the delegation that came from Saskatoon to Ottawa to present the resolution. The resolution which was passed at Saskatoon was first discussed at a meeting which was held in Regina and which was attended by the premiers of the three prairie provinces.

Agricultural Products Marketing Act Then the three premiers, together with the representatives of the farm organizations, came to Ottawa. When I speak of farm organizations, I am speaking not only of western organizations but of eastern ones. The Canadian Federation of Agriculture brought representatives here along with the three premiers and they presented the resolution which has just been read to the house.
One of the questions I asked them was as to whether they were arguing or suggesting that the present wheat board is not a producers board. There was not anyone who would come out definitely and say it was not a producers board, but they said it had been operating in a manner which was not entirely in the interests of the producer. I asked this question: What producers are you talking about? Are you talking about the producers of oats and barley out in western Canada or are you including the feeders of oats and barley in eastern Canada who are also farmers? Which are you speaking of? They intimated that they were trying to speak for all the producers, but there might be some doubt. Then I asked them this definite question: Are you opposed to the board, whether it is the wheat board or whatever board it may be, deciding that instead of selling grain to the feeders in Denmark, they are going to retain oats and barley in Canada in order to feed the livestock we have in this country? Or are you saying that we must sell the oats and barley at the highest price we can get, even if we take the oats and barley out of this country and leave our own feeders without feed grain? The answer I finally received was: We think you should sell it at the highest price you can get for it no matter where you sell it.
The natural position to take on that is that we have had experiences in this country over a long period of years in connection with growing grain. Our grain is grown in an area that is subject to drought, and there has not been a five-year period that I can recall in the time that I have been associated with western Canada when some one of the provincial governments did not have to ask for support from the federal government and from the railways in order to see to it that no grain was taken out of certain areas of western Canada at any price. If it were taken out, then the livestock in those areas would go without feed.
We have had conditions like that within the last three years. The provincial governments of Alberta and Saskatchewan have appealed to me as Minister of Agriculture to see to it that no grain was moved for several months at a time out of the area west of the Soo line, and that within the last three years. In this country I do not think you can have a control over coarse grain which would meet the con-

Then you must meet the condition that exists in another part of Canada where a surplus of grain may be shipped over from the United States at a lower price, or shipped in by boat from the Argentine at a lower price and sold on this market. Under those conditions you must not forget the fact that in order to pay that difference we must take money out of the treasury, which was paid into it by all the taxpayers of Canada. In other words it is impossible to operate the wheat board on the basis which is suggested in the resolution which was read this evening.
After we had these discussions I think they suggested that under certain circumstances they might go back and in the other two provinces pass the enabling legislation which was asked for last session. It had already been passed in Saskatchewan. It has since been passed in Alberta. At that time they said they would go back and consider passing it.
I understand it is under consideration in Manitoba.
If what they want in western Canada is the marketing of oats and barley through the wheat board they do not need the powers of this legislation at all in order to get it. They can get their marketing of oats and barley through the wheat board by enacting the legislation already enacted by Alberta and Saskatchewan and if it is enacted by Manitoba. I understand it is being introduced into the house now. speakeroldname: Hon. Lionel Chevrier (Minister of Transport) moved
subtopic: CONTROL OF INTERPROVINCIAL AND INTERNATIONAL OIL OR GAS PIPE LINES
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 190, respecting oil or gas pipe lines.
He said: The purpose of this bill is to provide for the control of interprovincial and international oil or gas pipe lines. There is, I believe, no doubt about the jurisdiction of parliament over international and interprovincial pipe lines. The British North America Act, in so far as both sections 91 and 92 are concerned, covers such a case, and the bill has the approval of the Department of Justice.
At the last session of parliament a bill was introduced in the other place to incorporate Western Pipe Lines. The purpose of that bill was to incorporate a company with power to construct and operate a pipe line for the transmission of natural gas from a point near Calgary to a point near Winnipeg, and also certain branch lines. After considerable discussion the bill was withdrawn by its promoters, and the reason given was that my officers held the view that, to give private companies power over interprovincial and international pipe lines, without some governing body, would be to create a position of chaos in a new and growing field; hence the decision to enact this enabling legislation.
The government has decided to recommend to parliament the enactment of a public statute of general application regulating the

Pipe Lines Act
transportation of natural gas and oil by means of pipe lines connecting two or more provinces, or extending beyond the limits of a province. The importance of the oil and natural gas industries to the economic welfare of Canada cannot be overemphasized. Light, heat and power are essential to our needs, and pipe lines are able to serve industry and the public by affording the cheapest and most convenient form of transportation of oil and natural gas.
The petroleum industry, with its diversified products, is a complicated business. The function of the pipe line in the organization of the oil industry is chiefly to serve large oil companies as an important part of their operation in the transformation of crude oil into the finished products ready for the market. Transportation by pipe line of crude oil to the refineries, and of refined oil products from the refineries to the market, is the most economic method of transportation yet devised. The large refineries and the pipe lines are integrated as the pipe lines afford cheap transportation from the oil fields to the refineries, and the refineries are necessary to the economic life of the pipe lines. Pipe lines are essentially one-way carriers and require a large capital investment which in turn needs a large and steady volume of business in order to pay fixed charges, maintenance and operating costs. The risk of shifting sources of supply and markets makes the corporate enterprises engaged in the oil refining business especially suited to the undertaking of building and operating pipe lines.
There are four major oil companies in Canada, British American, Imperial, McColl-Frontenac and Shell. I expect that the construction of pipe lines will be undertaken by subsidiaries of these companies in the near future. As the industry is competitive, I hope that other oil companies will also enter the field. There are now very few pipe lines in Canada extending beyond the limits of a province. There is the Montreal to Portland pipe line which was built during the war as a war measure. There is also a pipe line entering Canada at Sarnia, and I understand there is a pipe line crossing the international border between Alberta and Montana.
The attention of all Canada is now focused on the oil discoveries in Alberta which we hope will exceed our most optimistic expectations. The industry is spending a lot of money and effort to find the petroleum supplies of the future. These efforts are getting results which are most gratifying and a great tribute to the enterprise shown by the oil industry. The oil companies which are interested in the Alberta fields are to be congratulated on the effort, skill and enterprise shown in discovering this new source of supply. This country is fortunate in having people who are bold 
enough to risk their capital in an endeavour to open up these new sources of wealth. The potentialities of the oil industry in Canada are immense.
The new oil fields discovered in Alberta will require the construction of trunk pipe lines to carry the crude oil to refineries and the finished products from the refineries to the markets. Nature has also blessed the province of Alberta with abundant sources of natural gas that can be readily transmitted by pipe line to the great benefit of many communities using or desirous of using gas for light, heat and industrial purposes. I expect that these projected pipe lines will cross both provincial and international boundaries. The regulation of such pipe lines is undoubtedly within the jurisdiction of parliament, and the time is opportune for the enactment of a general act to regulate interprovincial and international oil and gas pipe lines.
The information which I have at the moment is that there are a number of private companies seeking to get special enactments for the purpose of proceeding almost immediately with the construction of these lines.

Perhaps I could refer briefly to those companies. At the moment I am aware of five, and there may be others. The five are: Interprovincial Pipe Lines; the Queont Pipe Line Company; Western Pipe Lines; Alberta Natural Gas Company; West-coast Transmission Company.
The first of these, the Interprovincial Pipe Lines, is a company sponsored by Imperial Oil Limited. It seeks authority to build pipe lines within or outside of Canada. The company proposes to build a pipe line from Edmonton to Regina as the first stage of its construction. During 1949, if the legislation which they seek is approved, I am informed that the Imperial Oil Company expects to spend between $9 and $10 million on the line between Edmonton and Regina which will run to a total cost estimated at $35 to $40 million. As the company's plans develop, other lines will be built including a line to a point on the international boundary for the purpose of exporting oil to the United States. Perhaps it is of interest to the house to know that the share capitalization of this company is $200 million.
The Queont Pipe Line Company contemplates the possibility of building an interprovincial trunk pipe line, and three of the larger Canadian oil companies have filed a petition for a private bill to cover these plans. It is understood that preliminary studies indicate that the cost of this line might run from

$15 million to $20 million. The information I have indicates that the greater part of that money would be expended in Canada.
Then there is the case of Western Pipe Lines. The first bill that came before the other place during the last session of parliament was withdrawn after its introduction. The sponsors of this bill have informed me that it will again be introduced this session with some changes. According to the information given by the promoters of this bill at the last session, it is proposed to build a pipe line for the transmission of natural gas from a point in the vicinity of Calgary to the cities of Winnipeg and St. Boniface. The cost of the project was estimated last year at approximately $48 million.
The Alberta Natural Gas Company proposes to build a gas pipe line from the province of Alberta across the mountains to Seattle, in the state of Washington, and Vancouver, British Columbia. The cost of building the line is estimated at approximately $100 million, and about one-half of this amount will be spent in Canada. The capital required for this project will, in the main, be raised in the United States and I understand that funds are assured. The principals who are backing this venture are geologists and engineers of long experience with undertakings of this kind and are well financed.
The last private company seeking a special act of incorporation is the West Coast Transmission Company. This company seeks to build a line for the transportation of natural gas from Alberta to British Columbia and the state of Washington. I am informed that the Westcoast Transmission Company Limited proposes to spend between $50 million and $100 million on the construction of a gas pipe line from the Alberta gas fields to Vancouver and Seattle. This money will be spent mostly in Canada and will be largely United States capital.
From what I have said it will appear to the house that substantial sums of money will be spent in this country, a sum totaling between $200 million and $250 million, if these private special acts are given approval. Provision is made in this bill, particularly in part two thereof, that the board may order or declare a company to be a common carrier. This part applies to oil pipe lines only and not to gas pipe lines. The reason that this part differentiates between gas and oil pipe lines in so far as being a common carrier is concerned is that natural gas pipe lines, by the nature of the commodity carried and the difficulty of storing the gas, do not lend themselves to the business of common carriers.
In the United States, where they have had more experience with pipe lines than we have
Pipe Lines Act
had in Canada, interstate oil pipe lines are regarded as public transportation agencies and they were placed in the category of common carriers by the Hepburn amendment to the interstate commerce act for the purpose of regulating rates and services. This was done to promote competition in the oil industry by requiring the major oil companies to permit other shippers the use of their lines. Economic superiority of the pipe line as a means of transporting oil over long distances by land routes affords great competitive advantages to an oil company owning a pipe line, but if independent oil companies can use the pipe line as a common carrier this advantage is much lessened. It appears, however, that the regulation in the United States of oil pipe lines as common carriers has not been extensive, which may be explained largely by the fact that the users of pipe lines are in most cases the owners. The powers of the interstate commerce commission over pipe lines under the Hepburn act have been exercised less than its powers over any other type of carrier subject to its jurisdiction.	[DOT]
A moment ago I referred to the distinction in the bill between a gas pipe line and an oil pipe line in so far as the liability as a common carrier is concerned. I may add here that the gas industry is regarded more in the light of a public utility than the oil industry, and more subject to price regulation; but on account of jurisdictional difficulties the bill does not impose any control over the price of gas purchased or sold. The bill gives the board power to order a company operating a gas pipe line to extend or improve its transportation facilities and to sell gas to any person or municipality engaged in the local distribution of gas to the public and for such purpose to construct branch lines to communities immediately adjacent to its pipe lines if the board finds that no undue burden will be placed upon the company thereby.
The bill is a relatively simple one and is composed of several parts. It has an interpretation section; it has a section dealing with the powers of the board; and the powers of the board of transport commissioners are, in so far as the pipe lines are concerned, almost the same as the powers contained in the Railway Act. A section deals with the powers of the company, and those are wide, giving to the company a list of general powers to take lands as set out in clause 7 of the bill. Part I deals with the location of the lines and applies equally to oil pipe lines and gas pipe lines. Sections 11, 12, 13 and 14 deal with the procedure before the board of transport commissioners.

I think I can easily refrain from referring to the clauses, Mr. Speaker. Let me say that the bill provides for the procedure before the board of transport commissioners. That procedure is for the applicant to file a plan. A plan having been filed, the board may grant leave to construct a line. The board can grant the order provided that certain details such as a book of reference, location of the line, the number of the lot and so forth, are filed with the board. That having been done, the board gives an order and the order must be registered in the registry office for the district or districts in which the line is located. There are provisions having to do with the taking of minerals and the protection thereof. Part III of the bill, as I intimated a moment ago, deals with the fact that oil companies may be made common carriers. I should have said that part II deals with oil lines whereas part III deals exclusively with gas lines. Then there is a part having to do with accounts and statistics, namely part IV.
In the other place there were one or two minor amendments which were made to the act, one having to do with interpretation and the other having to do with exemption with reference to branch lines. I recommend this bill to the house. In doing so, I trust that hon. members will bear in mind that there is great urgency for the passing of this act because of the fact that these private bills are awaiting the passage of this enabling legislation. While there is some urgency because of the importance of these projects, at the same time parliament is breaking new ground in the matter of general pipe line legislation, and the bill deserves the most careful consideration of the house.

subtopic: CONTROL OF INTERPROVINCIAL AND INTERNATIONAL OIL OR GAS PIPE LINES
speechtext:
The official opposition approve of the principle of this bill, Mr. Speaker, because we are strongly in favour of the development of the oil resources of Canada-provided of course that, once developed, they are wisely used. We believe that oil and iron can form the foundation upon which Canada could become a great world power. It will be remembered that there is no great power in the world today or in modern times which has not had a great production of iron and steel; together with oil they are of the utmost importance in these modern times.
The minister has said something about the oil and gas resources in the province of Alberta. I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, that 
the finding of oil in that province has been one of the most important developments in the life of this nation. I believe that by the end of this year there will be a production of crude oil in Alberta of approximately 100,000 barrels a day. If I am wrong in any of these figures, I would ask the minister to correct me. Apparently the quantity required in the three prairie provinces is only about 60,000 barrels per day. There will therefore be, by the end of the year, a surplus of about 40,000 barrels a day. I believe that the requirements of the whole of Canada are something like 290,000 barrels of crude oil per day. Hence Alberta production is now becoming an important factor in supplying the total requirements of Canada.
We hope that the result of this production in Alberta will mean the establishment of many industries in that province and also in the adjoining provinces. We hope too that this oil will eventually be used to cut down the requirements of coal in Ontario. As the house knows, one of the weak spots in the Canadian economy is that we have no coal in Ontario or in Quebec with the result that in both of these provinces we have to import great quantities of coal from the United States.

subtopic: CONTROL OF INTERPROVINCIAL AND INTERNATIONAL OIL OR GAS PIPE LINES
speechtext: And leave our own mines idle.

subtopic: CONTROL OF INTERPROVINCIAL AND INTERNATIONAL OIL OR GAS PIPE LINES
speechtext:
Yes, I am afraid in some cases the result is to leave Canadian mines idle in the more remote provinces. We do hope that it will be possible to bring this Alberta oil into Ontario and also into British Columbia. I see no reason why eventually it should not be piped down to the Pacific coast. It is likely also that there will be a surplus which of course can be sold in the United States. It is a very encouraging picture, Mr. Speaker. Not only is there oil in Alberta but we believe that there are also potential oil fields in the Peace river district of British Columbia and in Saskatchewan and the Northwest Territories.
As the minister has said, this is a new field of legislation for the Canadian parliament. It is certain to be a big field. We need only look to the United States where I believe they have a greater mileage of oil pipe lines than they have of railways. I may be wrong in that statement, but in any event they have a very large mileage in the United States.
Because this is a new type of legislation I submit that this proposed control law is of the utmost importance. The bill we are now considering is a key bill based, as the minister has said, on the fact that the pipe lines will cross interprovincial and international boundaries. I understood him to say that that is the reason it is considered that the Canadian parliament, as distinct from the provin-

cial legislatures, has the jurisdiction to introduce a control bill of this kind. The bill brings all these interprovincial and international oil and gas pipe lines under parliament. I believe also the government plans that all the companies must be incorporated under private acts of parliament.

speechtext: By special acts.

subtopic: CONTROL OF INTERPROVINCIAL AND INTERNATIONAL OIL OR GAS PIPE LINES
speechtext:
Incorporated by a special act of parliament. As the minister said, there are already five companies interested in applying for such acts. I will not take the time of the house to repeat the names of these companies, but I presume there will be more as time goes on.
The minister has already pointed out that the board of transport commissioners is to be made supreme in administering this act. That is a wise plan, because the board of transport commissioners is a judicial body, and it is wiser to put them in control rather than have the control placed directly in the hands of a department of government. But the minister said nothing at all about the interest of the provinces in these pipe lines.
I believe that the provinces of Canada, certainly the province of Alberta, are vitally interested in this legislation. I am afraid that the legislation will not work out as it is meant to unless there is the utmost cooperation with the provincial authorities.
I am going to suggest to the minister and to the house that when this bill receives second reading it be referred to a committee of the house. I presume the proper committee would be the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines. I suggest that it be referred to that committee for consideration. The same course should be followed with the special acts which are to be brought in in respect of the different companies. If such procedure is followed the result will be that the members of the house, the press and the Canadian public generally will have an opportunity to study the terms of the bill, and we may find in the end that we have the very best kind of legislation that can be enacted.
If the bill were referred to a committee of the house, witnesses could be called. For example, the provinces should be given the opportunity to make whatever representations they wish before this committee. Officials could be called from the Department of Transport. That was done in the other place, Mr. Speaker. There I believe the solicitor of the department appeared before the committee and also the solicitor of the board of transport commissioners. It would also be wise to call before that committee officials of the companies interested, namely,
Pipe Lines Act
the companies that propose to install these pipe lines.
In connection with the bill I should like to place before the government briefly, four or five considerations. We have not had this bill very long for study, and I do not pretend to have all the suggestions that could be made with respect to it. The first consideration is this. The oil and gas should be used in Canada as much as possible. I would point out to the minister that two of the five companies which he has named are proposing to pipe gas from Alberta down to the Pacific coast, but their main purpose is not to pipe gas to Vancouver but to pipe it to Seattle and Portland in the west coast states of the United States. There is a far bigger population in those two states than in British Columbia, and I believe that the intention is that the main line of these pipe lines will be to these states with a branch up to Vancouver.

speechtext: On a point of order, this bill does not provide that pipe lines shall go anywhere. It simply deals with general rules governing interprovincial and international pipe lines. My hon. friend is now talking about private bills that are being introduced in another place, and which will come here in due course. This bill does not provide for piping gas to any particular place.

If he could do that, surely I can. In his speech he said that the pipe lines were to go to Vancouver and Seattle.

subtopic: CONTROL OF INTERPROVINCIAL AND INTERNATIONAL OIL OR GAS PIPE LINES
speechtext:
The point I am making, Mr. Speaker, and I am amazed that the minister should interrupt, is that this oil and gas should be used to the greatest possible extent within our own country. I cite as an example the possibility that these two companies piping natural gas to the Pacific coast may be piping it primarily for the western United States rather than for British Columbia.
The second consideration which I think should be borne in mind is that the dominion government, having stepped into this field, will now be responsible for giving assistance to the provinces in the conservation of these natural resources. I believe this opens the door, or places some obligation at least upon the dominion government to help the provinces conserve these resources.
The third consideration-and this is a very important one-is that this development of

Pipe Lines Act
oil and natural gas must bring down the cost to the Canadian consumer. I submit that the development could be a great help in reducing the cost of living in Canada. There is not much use in Canada's developing vast quantities of oil and natural gas if our people are not going to have any benefit by way of reduced prices for those commodities.
That means that pipe lines should be installed in the most economical way possible. It seems to me some use should be made of the railway rights of way. For example, if pipe lines are to go to the Pacific coast, they will probably have to go through the Yellowhead pass or the Crowsnest pass. Are we to have new rights of way through all those hundreds of miles of mountain country, or is some use to be made of the railway rights of way? That is a point worthy of some thought. The railways have their maintenance staffs; they are already looking after their own rights of way; and surely there would be a great saving if, in so far as is reasonably possible, these pipe lines used railway rights of way. That would also mean far less interference with private property. Under the bill the companies are given the very widest powers of expropriation; they can go onto anyone's land and expropriate. I suggest that consideration be given to making use of railway rights of way.
I understand that this pipe line business is highly profitable; that very large profits can be made out of the operation of pipe lines. I must say 1 am somewhat surprised that the railways are not interested; that they have not stepped in to install at least some of these pipe lines.
A further consideration I place before the minister is that oil pipe lines at least must serve all comers. There is some provision in the bill that they must take oil from whoever offers it. I believe however that in the United States the terminology in the legislation provides that, where there is more oil than can be taken by a pipe line, the company owning the pipe line must take a fair share from everyone offering oil. One could describe it as carrying oil rateably. As I read the bill -and I have gone through it carefully-I do not find any such provision. In my view a provision of that kind should be inserted. Otherwise if one of the oil companies puts in a pipe line, and then has sufficient oil of its own to fill it, the independent operator will just be out of luck. That would be most unfair and, I suggest, should be provided against.
The minister has said that the natural gas lines, as distinguished from the oil lines, are not to be considered as public carriers. That may be a good plan, or it may not. Frankly 
at the present time I cannot understand why they should not both be made public carriers. However, I do not know enough about the business to be emphatic on the point.
The final consideration I place before the minister is that the government must move quickly to set up an efficient staff under the board of transport commissioners to handle the administration of this oil control bill. I should think that experienced oil men would have to be engaged. There would have to be inspectors. A whole new staff must be set up. I hope the control of the board of transport commissioners is not to be a mere formality. If that were to be so, the bill would have little value.
The administration of this measure is left to the board of transport commissioners, and that board must be in a position where it can do a real job. These companies will have to be watched. There will have to be efficient supervision by the board. It is a very busy organization at the present time, trying to settle freight rate questions; and just how it is going to step into this new field and give a proper lead in setting up control of oil and gas pipe lines, I do not see. Before the bill goes to committee I suggest the minister should explain what changes are proposed in the set-up of the board of transport commissioners in order that it might be able to handle this legislation.
Those are all the considerations I have to place before the house. I hope other members will put forward further suggestions. I am sure there are many hon. members in the house who know a great deal more about this subject than I do. The official opposition believe that the bill is of the utmost importance. We pledge our co-operation in getting it into the very best possible form, so that it will be of great benefit to the people of Canada as a whole.

Speaker, with much of what the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) has said, we in this group agree. We also agree that the principle of the bill should be endorsed on second reading, and that it should then be referred to the committee on railways, canals, and telegraph lines for further consideration.
As the minister has said, we are breaking new ground; and while there may be a rush in the matter, yet I do not think we can treat it lightly. In my view a committee of this house should deal with it fully. The minister mentioned a private bill introduced last year in another place, on the application of the western pipe lines. This bill received second reading in the other place and was referred to their committee on railways. I

had the privilege of sitting in at the hearings of that committee, and I may say that Alberta, Manitoba and Saskatchewan were represented, because they were the three provinces chiefly concerned. Those provinces were very much interested, in fact all provinces I think will be interested in the bill now before the house. I certainly think that all provinces should be given the opportunity to appear before a committee of this house in order to make representations and offer any objections they may have to the bill.
I believe that they do have objections. Last year the three provinces that I have mentioned were almost unanimous in their objections to the private bill which was then before the committee in the other place. For instance, the minister told us tonight that a pipe line would be considered a common carrier while a gas line would not be considered a common carrier. I think the provinces desire to make representations that a gas line should be considered a common carrier the same as a pipe line carrying oil.
As the speaker preceding me has said, some great powers are being given to these companies. They are to have the power of expropriation; they are to have the power of directing the registrars of deeds or registrars of land titles, as we call them in western Canada, to register deeds. There are provisions in connection with highway crossings. These are all provincial matters and I think the provinces should have an opportunity of making representations.
As the minister said, this is an important bill because the pipe lines will cross from one province to another. But even at that, does not the minister think that it should be declared in the bill that this is a work for the general good of Canada, as is required in the British North America Act? I am just throwing that out as a suggestion because I believe it would then be brought within the powers of this parliament.
As I say, we favour the principle of the bill. It is getting late and possibly some other hon. member may wish to speak. As I have to catch a train I shall waste no further time, but I hope that the minister will consent to the bill being referred to a committee as suggested by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green).
